Danmaku Unlimited 3 ist ein vertikal scrollender Bullet-Hell-Shooter (Shmup), der klassische Arcade-Intensität mit moderner Präsentation verbindet. Entwickelt von Doragon Entertainment, bietet er ein präzises, reaktionsbasiertes Spielerlebnis, das Geschick, Mustererkennung und Konzentration belohnt.

Das Spiel konzentriert sich auf reines Gameplay: Du steuerst ein Kampfschiff durch dichteste Kugelformationen und besiegst Gegner mit präzisem Schuss- und Laserfeuer. Das zentrale System, “Grazing”, belohnt riskantes Spiel – Kugeln knapp zu verfehlen lädt deine Trance-Leiste auf, wodurch du in einen verstärkten Modus mit massiver Feuerkraft wechseln kannst. Dadurch entsteht ein stetiger Rhythmus zwischen Risiko und Belohnung.

Jede Stage ist sorgfältig gestaltet, mit klar lesbaren Angriffsmustern und Bosskämpfen, die Timing und Musterverständnis fordern. Fehler werden sofort bestraft, aber auch sofort verstanden – das Lernen von Bewegungsrouten und Bullet-Formationen ist der Kern des Fortschritts.

Die Präsentation kombiniert traditionelle 2D-Spielmechanik mit 3D-Grafik und einem dynamischen Soundtrack der Band Blankfield, der das Tempo und die Intensität des Spiels perfekt unterstreicht. Explosionen, Farben und Bewegungen sind klar und präzise, nie chaotisch trotz der Bildschirmfülle.

Spielmodi wie Spirit Mode und Pure Mode erlauben unterschiedliche Herangehensweisen – der eine betont Punktesysteme und Combos, der andere reines Überleben und Präzision. Anpassbare Schwierigkeitsgrade machen das Spiel sowohl für Genre-Veteranen als auch für Einsteiger zugänglich, ohne an Anspruch zu verlieren.

Danmaku Unlimited 3 ist eine Hommage an klassische Bullet-Hell-Spiele wie DoDonPachi oder Ikaruga, aber mit klarer, moderner Struktur. Es ist kompromisslos fokussiert auf Reaktionsgeschwindigkeit, Musterbeherrschung und Flow – ein präzises, elegantes Beispiel für minimalistisches Arcade-Design.

Danmaku Unlimited 3 is the misunderstood and somewhat eccentric child from a marriage between a Touhou-style and Cave-like arcade STG; this however does not mean that DU3 doesn't have its place, because it most certainly does... and what a joy it is to behold.

DU3's greatest strengths lie with its presentation and ability to effortlessly fuse together two very different forms of STG's. Touhou-inspired shmups tend to focus on boss fights with fancy and mesmerizing bullet patterns -- or spell cards -- while Cave-like arcade STG's tend to focus more on chaotic levels with plenty of bombs, hypers, anarchy, and chest-thumping music from the beginning up until the very end of each stage. For reasons which escape me however, DU3's presentation take some time to appreciate; both enemies and even stage backgrounds may seem bland at first, but they're so full of easily overlooked detail.

DU3 is one of those games where the more you play, the more you see, and the more you appreciate. Which is a pity really, because I see many players picking DU3 up and putting it down mere hours later thinking that it is either too dull, not exciting enough, or doesn't offer anything extraordinary.

What was love-on-first-sight however was DU3's extremely sharp visuals. Both your hitbox and enemy bullets are extremely clear and easy to distinguish from the never-ending chaos and destruction; and critically, complex bullet patterns employ well thought out color palettes which make identifying individual sub-patterns a breeze. Even when patterns begin to aggressively overlap on higher difficulties it is always easy to distinguish one pattern from another and to quickly identify and establish an escape route; this means that spell cards are often extremely fair despite being outlandishly difficult at times.

It isn't just the boss fights which shine in DU3 however; stages themselves are very well thought out with well choreographed enemy formations and attack patterns complemented by beautiful level design and harmonizing special effects and music.

Behind all this grace and beauty however is an immensely hardcore and punishing game, even by STG standards. For starters, DU3 doesn't really believe in invulnerability frames; you can get hit repeatedly so quickly and lose all your extends in absolutely no-time that you'll be scratching your head first in confusion, then disbelief, and ultimately awe. Next up, DU3 employs an all-or-nothing approach to scoring: your score multiplier -- which does NOT counter stop -- is increased by grazing bullets, which is fine, but this multiplier can be carried all the way from the second you start, through boss fights, to the end-of-stage scorecard. What this means is getting hit just once (which resets your multiplier all the way back to zero) or even using a bomb (which cuts it in half) is more often than not run-ending when playing for score, as a multiplier of 10,000 becomes a very big deal when clearing even just one additional pattern.

DU3 also has a habit of augmenting its mesmerizing bullet patterns with speed and this results in one heck of an adrenaline-rush; not only do you need to be able to work well with Touhou-style spell cards, but you're going to have to be snappy as well as boss phases transition extremely quick.

With all that said though, DU3 is still an approachable and somewhat accessible game as the easier difficulties are well balanced and will still make you feel like an absolute champion. And for those who are looking to get better, I genuinely feel that each increase in difficulty is a very natural evolution from the previous one which results in earlier difficulties being a solid foundation for the next tier up. This is a trait I'm always fond of as maintaining a certain degree of familiarity is a kind of fairness which tends to compliment what is otherwise an extremely challenging game to master.

All-in-all Danmaku Unlimited 3 is a proper danmaku in every sense of the genre and it's always delightful to see more STG's embrace the mesmerizing beauty of bullet patterns which are more typically associated with Touhou-style shmups. What an awesome game!~

I’m frankly amazed by the number of ways this game manages to be a disappointing followup to Danmaku Unlimited 2. I thought DU2 was a solid shmup, and DU3 looks cleaner and has a much cooler soundtrack. But my praise ends there. 

The UI in Danmaku Unlimited 3 is broken in several places. Ship selection often doesn’t work, forcing you to play ship type A-A even when you pick other types. Pressing continue to go to the next stage sometimes plays a looping animation that delays loading. And the game repeatedly asks you to replay the tutorial since “it appears this is your first time playing,” even when it most definitely isn’t. 

The gameplay takes inspiration from the worst aspects of CAVE’s mostly storied lineup. Spirit Mode, for example, adopts the cancel-on-kill mechanic from Espgaluda II Black Label, neutering the threat of most non-boss enemies in DU3 to the point that many stages practically play themselves if you sit in the middle and hold fire. A variation of the awful laser wheels from DaiFukkatsu that nobody wanted to see ever again also show up in multiple stages here, along with some rather poorly-communicated wall interactions that belong in a horizontal shooter, not a bullet hell. And the bosses have too many phases, many of which drag on for way too long.

All in all, this game is only mostly functional and only partly fun. I would recommend other shmups over this one any day of the week. My personal favorites on Steam are Mushihimeama, Gunvein, and Blue Revolver, all danmaku games like DU3. Devil Blade Reboot is also great if you want something simpler, and Eigengrau is an underrated puzzle-shmup hybrid that might also be worth your time.

I want to love every shmup I've never played before, especially since I've rediscovered my love for this neglected genre after burning myself out on AAA movie-games, walking sims, Simon-says mechanics and all-around boring non-gameplay-fests that define modern gaming. It's been such a blast, I've even held myself to purchasing shmups at full retail price as often as possible to show my support, including recent compilations, new indie releases and M2's PS4-exclusive imports. This game is among those I bought at retail cost and no, regardless of my review, I'm not refunding it.

But [i]DU3[/i] falls short for me for two huge reasons I keep coming back to play a game: the audio design and the art design.

Whether or not you like the genre of music they went for, Blankfield's soundtrack pummels the ears from the word GO. This [b]trve cvlt[/b] instrumental metal music amuses at first, but quickly becomes tiring on the ears. And considering how draining an intense shmup session can be at higher difficulties (let alone multiple runs), music that aims to exhaust the ears doesn't help the player... it hinders them. And even if the style is up your alley, where's the memorable melodies that characterize indie shmups? Where's the exciting panache of an [i]Andro Dunos II[/i], a [i]Ginga Force[/i], an [i]Eschatos[/i], a [i]Rolling Gunner[/i], or a [i]Blue Revolver?[/i] All those shumps contain musical earworms that pop in my head at random, which is surely indicative of higher art. But the best I can recall here is the drummer's blast beats during a boss battle. (Not exactly a musical revelation.) Even worse, when you swap in your own music or turn it off entirely, you'll notice how weak the sound effects in this game are. They just simply don't have the impact they should. Frankly, they sound wimpy. And that's bad in an action game.

Speaking of, Doragon advertises this as a "Classic Japanese Bullet Hell Action" game... yet for all its polish, it lacks all the aspects of great art design that gave those Japanese classics the status they rightfully deserve. Strictly taking away the bullet hell part, you're telling me that [b]visually[/b] this reminds you of a CAVE game, a Raizing game, or a Psikyo game? This reminds you of a Taito, a Toaplan, a Treasure, or even a Seibu Kaihatsu? Then where's the tasty art designs at? Where's the wild explosions? Where's the color and definition? Where's [i]the style[/i] in this game?! I mean, it's not like they have to plaster the game with fan-service-y waifus, but [i]DU3[/i] has a sterile, comparably dull visual design. This doesn't remind me of Japanese shmups, it reminds me of EastAsiaSoft ones!

Ultimately, both of those issues clash rather than unify, which (to me) is a pitiful waste of good gameplay. There's a bitter irony that this game really is the opposite of AAA development; whereas big-budget titles effortlessly nail every single thing except a consistently satisfying gameplay loop, [i]Danmaku Unlimited 3[/i] gets said loop right, but nothing else. (In that sense, it reminds me of another fun game with unappealing aesthetics: [i]Pixeljunk Monsters.[/i]) And games like that remind me more than ever of how important [b]all[/b] the elements of a game are, otherwise even the target audience themselves won't stick around for the long haul.

So, check out a no-commentary, full-game run on YT first. See if the style appeals to you and go from there.

I really enjoyed Danmaku Unlimited 2, but many of the elements I liked about 2 have been stripped away 'for beginners'.  Yet, I find Danmaku Unlimited 3 far less beginner friendly.

The game play is roughly the same as the previous.  You have a regular shot and a more powerful shot with slower movement.  Plus, bombs that serve as shields if hit.  Finally, you have a Trance/hyper shot that fires automatically once the meter builds from grazing (getting close to enemy projectiles) or absorbing their 'shadow' when canceled typically from destroying the enemy ship that fired them.  

It's the automatic part that feels bad.  It can go off when it really is of no use unless you purposely avoid building up that last little bit.  Which is less beginner friendly than just allowing the player to release it on command.  And far more annoying to have to work around it.

Danmaku Unlimited 2 already had boss battles with more and longer lasting phases than I prefer.  Danmaku Unlimited 3 feels like there's more and they are longer.  I don't know if that's true, but I do find my mind wandering as I wait for the next phase.  Sure, there's bullet patterns to dodge.  But I either know how to dodge it or I really don't.  The game forcing me to run through it for several more seconds than most bullet hells I've played only changes that I get tired of waiting for the next phase to start.  And I'd think I was doing something wrong as how slow damage was applied if I didn't have to struggle to setup my controls.

And struggle I did.  I'm weird in that I like to use an 8-button Sega Genesis controller when I can.  Danmaku Unlimited 3 doesn't allow me to without the use of a MayFlash Magic-S Pro 2.  Which isn't ideal, but some STGs don't even let me get that far.  However, remapping keys is strange in this game.  The beam shot doesn't work unless I hold down the regular shot and the beam shot at the same time.  Pause is what's listed to fire bombs.  And the only other thing that can be re-mapped is the menu button.  It took me a good while to release I could manually use bombs.  I was beginning to wonder why the game called the bombs at all since up until that point, I thought they just let you take extra hits and they didn't even create smaller explosion closer to your ship like some shmups do that also have this feature.

All in all, I can't recommend Danmaku Unlimited 3.  If feels like a big step back from Danmaku Unlimited 2, and just claims that step back was in the name of being beginner friendly.  Which I don't think it is.  As I found Danmaku Unlimited 2 to also be a tad less difficult on the Easy setting.  Allowing novice players to get to play more than the first couple stages.  

I'm not a very good shmup player admittedly, but I have a very tough time getting to Stage 3 on Easy after an hour of play.  Where actual shmups I would recommend to beginner players, I'm usually working on beating the final boss (on Easy) if not beating the the game.  And Danmaku Unlimited 3 does not inspire me to continue to try either.  I'm certainly not enticed to unlock different firing modes as deep into the game as it wants me to unlock them.

[h1] INTRODUCTION [/h1]

Danmaku Unlimited 3 is a bullet hell shmup that stands out with its bright, glossy visuals and catchy soundtrack. This series of shmups remains one of my favorites and 3 separates itself off from not only DU2, but also from a lot of shmups I've played in general.


[h1] PATTERNS [/h1]

Danmaku Unlimited 3 sets itself apart from other shmups I've played by having pretty unique bullet patterns that are generally focused more on tight precision than reaction time. The game loves to force you into a small corner of the screen and demand tiny inputs inside little amounts of screen space, and then suddenly demand you move out of that area into another tight zone. Lasers are used often by both enemies and bosses and the game likes to throw bullets at you from multiple directions at once. There's a few waves in the game I felt were a little silly, and I'm not big on enemies that have too much health to kill on time, which in later stages is abused often, but I haven't come across any pattern that didn't make sense or felt unfair. The bullet patterns are a big selling point of this game to me, and it does things very creatively.


[h1] DIFFICULTY [/h1]


 There are 4 difficulties and 2 modes to play through, and I want to acknowledge that the difficulty of DU3 is a *huge* increase from the second game, the beginner recommended medium difficulty was even surprisingly rough and felt more comparable to the second game's third highest difficulty. 


[h1] PRESENTATION [/h1]


It's crazy how much visual splendor this game gets away with while still being perfectly visible and playable. Ships have large explosion and everything has a glow to it, the backgrounds you play on are gorgeous and everything is *very* colorful. Despite all this, the bullets are *never* obscured by the background or the other ships and I never had any trouble seeing what I was doing, and this is something I noticed bullet hell games struggle with sometimes. The music is absolutely incredible and feels kinda cinematic and high energy fitting the intense battles you're dealing with. 

[h1] CONCLUSION [/h1]

If there's a bullet hell shmup you should play and might have missed, it's Danmaku Unlimited 3. The game does what it wants to perfectly, and is a solid entry to anyone's bullet hell library

Danmaku Unlimited 3 represents a simple, but solid and highly enjoyable foray into SHMUPs.  This is a game with tight controls, clear visuals, great hitboxes (on bullets with sharp outlines but also the centroid of your ship), and an adrenaline-pumping heavy metal soundtrack with tons of DJENT!  This is a short game, and it's a pretty hard game.  You have 4 difficulties in Spirit Mode with some easy options, but only 2 quite hard difficulties in Graze Mode (which is already harder so it's double harder).  It's a fun game, you fly around in a spaceship and shoot other spaceships.  If you don't really like SHMUPs, this game will not change your mind though.

Details: Danmaku Unlimited 3 is a vertical shmup without any terrain or set hazards.  It has inconsequential backdrops, and every stage is basically the same except for enemies, midbosses, and the bosses.  It is similar to many Arcade-style SHMUPs and the bullet patterns do become semi-crazy, but not nearly as crazy as some other games on Steam or in arcades.  The scoring AND the survival is entirely based around "grazing" bullets by getting fairly close but without getting hit.  When enemies are destroyed all the time in Spirit Mode, and some of the time in Graze Mode, their current on-screen bullets are turned into harmless blue spirits.  You can touch these to gain points and fill up your super meter... but by getting close enough to touch them you also graze them.  Absorbing tons of spirits is the key to a high score, because you can use your super meter to enter Trance Mode and do massive damage while swimming in yummy golden gems and points.  However this gameplay design has an unfortunate caveat: If you play poorly and don't graze much (because you're trying to survive), then you have no chance of even a remotely decent score and no ability to use Trance Mode very often at all.  It's very all-or-nothing.

The art is clear, the music is nice, and the game is very straightforward and fair to the player.  Generally speaking it's clear what you want to do, and clear what you did wrong when you get hit. That said, this game is extremely difficult on the hardest mode (Graze Mode / True Difficulty) and it is not for the faint of heart.  I can't 1cc that level of difficulty but I still enjoy this game and recommend it.
